title: Set 1: Actors and Roles under RA 10173
description: Match each key actor with their legal definition or statutory responsibility.

pairs.right: Individual whose personal, sensitive, or privileged data is processed
pairs.explanation: The individual who owns the personal data protected under RA 10173.

pairs.right: Decides what data is processed, why, and how (accountable under Sec. 21)
pairs.explanation: Holds ultimate accountability for processing compliance under Sec. 21.

pairs.right: Third party that processes data for and on behalf of a controller (e.g. cloud host)
pairs.explanation: Operates under the contractual instructions and oversight of the PIC.

pairs.right: Monitors organizational compliance and serves as contact point for the NPC
pairs.explanation: Designated corporate officer responsible for privacy compliance.

pairs.right: Regulatory agency that enforces RA 10173 and issues circulars
pairs.explanation: The central government body regulating personal data protection in the Philippines.

title: Set 2: Privacy Theories and Scholars
description: Match each scholar or theorist with their foundational concept or framework.

pairs.right: The right to be let alone (freedom from unwarranted intrusion)
pairs.explanation: Harvard Law Review article establishing the modern legal concept of privacy.

pairs.right: Control over information (individual determination of self-disclosure)
pairs.explanation: Author of 'Privacy and Freedom', focusing on individual control and consent.

pairs.right: Contextual Integrity (data flow must conform to contextual norms)
pairs.explanation: Framework examining whether information transmission adheres to origin norms.

pairs.right: Privacy by Design (7 foundational engineering principles)
pairs.explanation: Former Ontario Information & Privacy Commissioner who pioneered PbD.

pairs.right: System Safety: 'Which control was missing?' instead of 'Who broke it?'
pairs.explanation: Accident analysis focusing on structural and architectural safety controls.

title: Set 3: Rights of the Data Subject
description: Match each data subject right with its statutory safeguard under RA 10173.

pairs.right: Refuse data processing, including direct marketing or profiling
pairs.explanation: Sec. 16: Right to withhold consent from unauthorized data utilization.

pairs.right: Demand correction of inaccurate or incomplete records in the system
pairs.explanation: Sec. 16: Ensuring the accuracy and integrity of personal information.

pairs.right: Suspend, withdraw, or order removal of data from the system
pairs.explanation: Sec. 16: Purging data when unlawful, obsolete, or when consent is withdrawn.

pairs.right: Obtain electronic, structured copies to transfer data to another platform
pairs.explanation: Sec. 18: Enables seamless migration of digital records across service providers.

pairs.right: Receive indemnification for damages sustained due to unlawful processing
pairs.explanation: Sec. 16: Right to financial compensation for injuries caused by statutory violations.

title: Set 4: Statutory Penalties and Sections
description: Match each criminal offense with its corresponding section in RA 10173.

pairs.right: Unauthorized Processing of Personal or Sensitive Information
pairs.explanation: 1-3 yrs (PI) / 3-6 yrs (SPI); fines up to ₱4,000,000.

pairs.right: Access Due to Negligence (failure to implement security controls)
pairs.explanation: 1-3 yrs (PI) / 3-6 yrs (SPI); fines up to ₱4,000,000.

pairs.right: Improper Disposal of Personal or Sensitive Information
pairs.explanation: 6 mos-2 yrs (PI) / 1-3 yrs (SPI); fines up to ₱1,000,000.

pairs.right: Concealment of Security Breach involving Sensitive Data
pairs.explanation: 1.5-5 yrs imprisonment; fines ranging from ₱500,000 to ₱1,000,000.

pairs.right: Large Scale: Maximum penalty imposed when 100+ individuals are affected
pairs.explanation: Automatically mandates the maximum penalty in the prescribed range.

title: Set 5: Forms of Intellectual Property Protection (RA 8293)
description: Match each form of intellectual property with what it protects, how it arises, and its statutory duration.

pairs.right: Protects expression, not ideas; arises automatically upon creation (Life + 50 years)
pairs.explanation: Covers source code, documentation, and digital assets automatically upon creation.

pairs.right: Protects statutory inventions; arises only by formal government grant (20 years from filing)
pairs.explanation: Covers novel, inventive, and industrially applicable technical processes.

pairs.right: Protects confidential, valuable business information; arises by maintaining secrecy (Indefinite)
pairs.explanation: Covers proprietary algorithms and customer data kept strictly confidential.

pairs.right: Protects distinctive signs, names, and logos; arises by registration and use (Renewable indefinitely)
pairs.explanation: Protects commercial brand identity and distinguishes goods or services.

pairs.right: Statutory defense weighed against 4 factors where attribution and education are not automatic exemptions
pairs.explanation: Assessed by purpose, nature, amount used, and potential market effect.

title: Set 6: Software Licence Families and Legal Obligations
description: Match each software license family with its legal permissions, requirements, and product consequences.

pairs.right: Permits any use without restrictions; imposes no downstream legal obligations
pairs.explanation: Copyright is completely waived, allowing unrestricted commercial and private use.

pairs.right: Permits commercial use and modification; requires retaining copyright and license notices
pairs.explanation: Highly suitable for commercial proprietary software with minimal notice obligations.

pairs.right: Permits linking in larger works; requires publishing modifications to the component itself
pairs.explanation: Proprietary applications may link to the library, but library modifications must be shared.

pairs.right: Requires the entire distributed derivative work to be published under the same copyleft terms
pairs.explanation: Can force proprietary software developers to release their complete source code.

pairs.right: Conveys no permission whatsoever; silence implies zero legal right to copy or use
pairs.explanation: Code published publicly without an explicit license cannot be lawfully integrated.

title: Set 7: Cybercrime Offences and Ordinary Conduct Exposure (RA 10175)
description: Match each cybercrime concept or ordinary IT practice with why it carries criminal exposure.

pairs.right: Highest practitioner risk; covers illegal access, interception, and data/system interference
pairs.explanation: Section 4(a) offenses resemble ordinary penetration testing and IT administration.

pairs.left: Retaining access after leaving a role
pairs.right: Authorization ends when the role ends; continued access constitutes access without right
pairs.explanation: The failure of IT to revoke an account does not grant ongoing lawful permission.

pairs.right: Authority to grant system access rests with the organization, not the account holder
pairs.explanation: An employee cannot lawfully delegate or transfer organizational access credentials.

pairs.left: Editing a URL to view other records (IDOR)
pairs.right: The absence of a technical barrier is not the presence of lawful permission
pairs.explanation: Flawed server authorization checks do not authorize accessing other users' data.

pairs.left: Scanning a network you do not own
pairs.right: Reconnaissance and port scanning may itself fall within defined unauthorized conduct
pairs.explanation: Automated network probing against third-party systems without consent triggers liability.

title: Set 8: Security Testing Protocols and Valid Authorization
description: Match each security testing standard with its mandatory legal requirement under RA 10175.

pairs.right: Must strictly precede the act; post-discovery consent does not retroactively legitimize access
pairs.explanation: Consent obtained after finding a flaw does not cure a completed illegal access offense.

pairs.right: Must originate from the data owner or corporate officer, not solely the system administrator
pairs.explanation: System administrators lack unilateral legal authority to permit security testing.

pairs.right: Probing without permission remains an offence; reporting afterwards is mitigation, not a defence
pairs.explanation: Helpful intent and vulnerability reporting reduce penalties but do not negate guilt.

pairs.right: Explicitly excludes third-party SaaS and shared cloud hosting from unauthorized scanning
pairs.explanation: Clients cannot authorize testing of cloud services they merely use and do not own.

pairs.right: Written charter defining scope, targets, methods, and contacts that protects testing professionals
pairs.explanation: This formal pre-testing document distinguishes a security auditor from a criminal defendant.
